The three concession areas offer opportunities for local and international companies to undertake geological surveys, exploration programmes and mineral resource assessments

Staff Writer ,  TradeArabia

Oman’s Ministry of Energy and Minerals has offered three new mining concession areas covering a combined 2,062 square kilometres, aiming to attract international investment, expand mineral exploration and support the development of an integrated mining industry.

The announcement was made during Oman’s participation in the International Mining and Resources Conference and Expo in Sydney, Australia, where the Ministry joined six companies operating in the minerals sector to showcase the Sultanate’s geological potential and investment opportunities.

The three concession areas offer opportunities for local and international companies to undertake geological surveys, exploration programmes and mineral resource assessments, paving the way for future mining projects subject to technical and economic feasibility studies.

Concession Area 25-C covers 627 square kilometres, with preliminary geological data indicating potential deposits of manganese, nickel and laterite ores.

Area 25-F spans 830 square kilometres and has potential for manganese, nickel and laterite, while Area 22-C extends across 605 square kilometres and contains geological indicators of copper, chromite and gold, alongside marble and basalt.

The Ministry’s participation in the three-day event also aims to strengthen cooperation with Australian and international companies in advanced mining technologies and promote investment across the mining value chain, from exploration and resource assessment to mine development, ore processing and manufacturing.

Mohsin Hamad Al Hadhrami, Undersecretary of the Ministry of Energy and Minerals, said Oman’s participation reflects its strategy to increase the minerals sector’s contribution to economic diversification and move beyond resource exploration and extraction towards an integrated mining industry driven by investment, modern technologies and specialised expertise.

He stressed that mineral wealth alone does not generate prosperity, noting that its economic benefits depend on investment, knowledge and technology to transform natural resources into productive projects, competitive industries and sustainable economic opportunities.

Al Hadhrami invited international companies and investors to explore the newly offered concessions and establish long-term partnerships that support resource development, technology transfer and the competitiveness of Oman’s mining sector.

He added that the Ministry is working to improve the regulatory and investment environment, simplify procedures and expand digital services to facilitate the progression of projects from exploration and assessment to development and production.

These efforts also include adherence to environmental standards, occupational health and safety requirements, the development of national skills and greater participation by Omani companies and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), supporting in-country value and the objectives of Oman Vision 2040.

Oman’s mineral potential is underpinned by geological diversity and formations dating back approximately 900 million years. Among its most significant geological features is the Samail Ophiolite, one of the world’s most important exposures of oceanic crust and upper mantle.

The country’s identified mineral resources and geological indicators include copper, chromium, gold, nickel, manganese, zinc, lead, gypsum, limestone, dolomite, marble, silica, silica sand, gabbro, basalt, quartzite, clay and salts.

While some resources are commercially exploited, others remain at the exploration and assessment stages, offering opportunities for new projects and downstream industries.

At the Sydney exhibition, Oman’s pavilion is presenting the available concession areas, existing projects and investment services, providing investors with direct access to Ministry representatives and participating companies.

Details of the opportunities and application requirements are available through the Ministry’s Taqa digital platform.

The latest offering follows broader efforts to strengthen Oman’s mining investment framework over the past five years.

During this period, 28 mining concession areas were awarded for the exploration and development of various minerals.

The Ministry also improved regulatory frameworks, introduced an occupational health and safety manual and established the Oman Minerals Trading Company to regulate ore trading and marketing.

Digitalisation has been another priority, with the Taqa platform enabling investors to submit and track applications and access available investment opportunities, improving transparency and concession management.

The sector has also recorded stronger economic performance. Mining revenues grew by 39 per cent in 2025 compared with 2024, reflecting the expansion of mining activities, the entry of copper production projects into operation and the advancement of several concession areas towards development and production.

The Mazoon Copper Mine project is among the anticipated developments expected to support future production and stimulate related mining activities and services.

Through the new concessions and continued regulatory reforms, Oman aims to attract specialised expertise, increase the value generated from its mineral resources and establish mining as a more significant contributor to economic diversification and sustainable growth under Oman Vision 2040.-OGN/TradeArabia News Service
